# Job Chapter 1 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 416r–416v | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/JOB_001_page_001.jpg, JOB_001_page_002.jpg

---

**1** In the land of Uz there lived a man named Job. He was a man of complete integrity, who lived an upright life, feared God, and stayed far from evil. **2** He had seven sons and three daughters. **3** He owned seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred donkeys — along with a huge number of servants. He was the greatest man among all the people of the east.

**4** His sons would take turns hosting feasts in their homes, each on his appointed day, and they would invite their three sisters to come and eat and drink with them. **5** When the round of feasting was over, Job would send for them and perform a purification rite. He would get up early in the morning and offer a burnt offering for each of them, thinking, "Perhaps my children have sinned and dishonored God in their hearts." This was Job's regular practice.

**6** One day the heavenly beings came to present themselves before the LORD, and the Accuser came with them. **7** "Where have you come from?" the LORD asked the Accuser. "From patrolling the earth," he replied, "roaming back and forth across it."

**8** Then the LORD said to the Accuser, "Have you noticed my servant Job? There is no one on earth like him — a man of complete integrity, who fears God and stays far from evil." **9** The Accuser answered, "Does Job fear God for nothing? **10** Haven't you placed a protective wall around him, his household, and everything he owns? You have blessed everything he does, and his wealth has spread across the land. **11** But reach out and take away everything he has — and he will curse you to your face!"

**12** "Very well," the LORD said to the Accuser. "Everything he has is in your power. But do not lay a hand on the man himself." So the Accuser left the LORD's presence.

**13** One day, while Job's sons and daughters were feasting and drinking wine at the oldest brother's house, **14** a messenger rushed to Job with this news: "The oxen were plowing and the donkeys grazing nearby, **15** when the Sabeans raided us! They stole the animals and killed the servants with swords. I am the only one who escaped to tell you!"

**16** While he was still speaking, another messenger arrived: "Fire from God blazed down from the sky and burned up the sheep and the servants! I am the only one who escaped to tell you!"

**17** While he was still speaking, yet another arrived: "Three bands of Chaldean raiders swept down on the camels and carried them off! They killed the servants with swords. I am the only one who escaped to tell you!"

**18** While he was still speaking, still another arrived: "Your sons and daughters were feasting at the oldest brother's house, **19** when suddenly a mighty wind swept in from the desert and struck the four corners of the house. It collapsed on the young people and they are all dead. I am the only one who escaped to tell you!"

**20** Job stood up, tore his robe, and shaved his head. Then he fell to the ground in worship. **21** "Naked I came from my mother's womb," he said, "and naked I will return. The LORD gave and the LORD has taken away. Praise the name of the LORD."

**22** In all of this, Job did not sin or blame God for anything.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**The wager in heaven:** The chapter presents one of the Bible's most daring theological scenarios — God himself initiates the test by drawing the Accuser's attention to Job. The suffering that follows is not punishment for sin but a test of whether goodness can exist without reward. This premise dismantles the simple equation that dominates much of the Old Testament: obey and prosper, disobey and suffer.

**The Accuser's question:** "Does Job fear God for nothing?" (v.9) — this is the question the entire book exists to answer. It asks whether genuine, disinterested piety is possible, or whether all human devotion is ultimately transactional.

**The cascade of messengers:** The narrative genius of verses 13-19 is the relentless pacing. Four messengers, four catastrophes, and the refrain "I alone have escaped to tell you" — the repetition creates an almost unbearable rhythm of loss. By the fourth messenger, the reader knows what is coming before the words arrive.

*— PNEUMA*
